record.context_brief: Highly connected graphs with highly connected spanning bipartite subgraphs.
record.original_question: For each integer k >= 1, is it true that every (2k - 1)-connected graph contains a spanning bipartite subgraph that is k-connected?

evidence.quote: Is it true that every (2k - 1)-connected graph has a k-connected spanning bipartite subgraph?

artifact.self_contained_problem:
A graph $G$ is said to be $m$-connected if it has more than $m$ vertices and remains connected after the removal of any set of fewer than $m$ vertices. A spanning subgraph of $G$ is a subgraph containing every vertex of $G$. A graph is bipartite if its vertex set can be partitioned into two parts so that every edge has one endpoint in each part.

Question: For every integer $k \geq 1$, is it true that every $(2k-1)$-connected graph $G$ contains a spanning bipartite subgraph that is $k$-connected?
artifact.status_search_result: This is a conjecture commonly attributed to Thomassen. It remains open in general. Recent work (e.g., a 2024 Electronic Journal of Combinatorics paper, "Highly Connected Graphs Have Highly Connected Spanning Bipartite Subgraphs") establishes that every t-connected graph has a k-connected spanning bipartite subgraph for some t = t(k,n) bounded above by a function such as O(k^2 log n), but the linear bound 2k-1 (independent of n) is not known. Thus the original question is unresolved.

status_evidence.title: Highly Connected Graphs Have Highly Connected Spanning Bipartite Subgraphs
status_evidence.snippet: Improves bounds on f(k,n), the smallest t such that every t-connected n-vertex graph has a k-connected spanning bipartite subgraph; Thomassen conjectured f(k,n) is bounded by a function of k.
status_evidence.claim: The bounded-by-function-of-k conjecture remains open; only weaker (n-dependent) bounds are known.

status_evidence.title: On a Conjecture of Thomassen
status_evidence.snippet: Discusses Thomassen's conjecture related to k-connected spanning bipartite subgraphs.
status_evidence.claim: The conjecture is referenced as an unresolved problem of Thomassen.
